title: Screen Time at Age 1 and 6 Tied to Lower Grades and Weaker Memory Later
summary:
Screens are everywhere, and young children are using them more than ever. But a new longitudinal study—one that follows the same people over time—suggests that when kids start heavy screen use might be just as important as how much they use.

Researchers from Inserm and the National University of Singapore tracked 502 children from infancy to age 10.5, using data from the GUSTO birth cohort. Parents reported their kids' screen time at six different ages. The team then compared that with academic performance at age 9 and working memory—the ability to hold and manipulate information in your mind—at age 10.5.

The results, published in the World Journal of Pediatrics, showed that higher screen exposure during infancy and around age 6 was associated with poorer academic outcomes and weaker working memory. The strongest link was at age 1. "The effect sizes we saw at age 1 were the largest among all time points we examined," the authors said. "That suggests early infancy may be a window of heightened sensitivity, when the developing brain is particularly vulnerable to the displacement of learning interactions by screen time."

Interestingly, screen use at ages 2 and 3 showed no significant link, but the association re-emerged at age 6—right when children enter formal schooling, facing new demands on attention and memory.

The researchers emphasize that "less is better" for screen exposure. An extra hour a day might not affect one child noticeably, but across a population, it could shift many kids toward poorer outcomes. They also note that screen duration alone doesn't capture everything—future studies should look at content quality, device type, and whether parents watch alongside.

These findings align with WHO and American Academy of Pediatrics guidelines, which recommend avoiding screens before 18-24 months and limiting to under one hour daily for ages 2-5. For parents, the takeaway is clear: early childhood is a sensitive period, and reducing screen time—especially at age 1 and around school entry—could have long-term benefits for learning and memory.
why_it_matters: This study points to specific ages when kids' brains may be most vulnerable to heavy screen use, which matters for families, schools, and policymakers setting screentime guidance. It also raises questions about what young children lose when screens replace interactive learning.

background_read: Longitudinal studies follow the same people over many years, which makes it possible to see how early experiences connect with later learning and memory.
GUSTO (Growing Up in Singapore Towards Healthy Outcomes) is a long-running birth-cohort study in Singapore that has tracked children and their families for years.
The new analysis was led by scientists at Inserm (France's national institute for health and medical research) and the National University of Singapore (a leading public university).
Earlier screen-time research has linked very early screen exposure with language delays and attention issues, though many experts stress that content and parental involvement also matter.

The World Health Organization (WHO), the United Nations' health agency, and the American Academy of Pediatrics, the main organization of U.S. children's doctors, both recommend limiting screens at young ages.

perspectives.description: For parents and health experts, the study offers a clear, actionable message: cutting screen time in infancy and around school entry could protect memory and grades. It reinforces existing guidelines with specific age windows.

The findings also sound a warning: screen exposure at an early age may displace the face-to-face interactions and play that young brains need. Children from homes with fewer alternatives may be especially affected, making this a fairness issue.

As an observational study, it can show links but not prove that screens caused the poorer outcomes. Family factors, sleep, and content type all matter, so the effect of screen time alone is probably modest.

Future studies should dig into content quality, device type, and whether parents watch alongside kids. The next step could be designing programs that help families reduce screens during the most sensitive windows and testing whether memory and grades improve.
